components.name: list item
components.description:
What the Component Does?

Represents one item in a list, combining a primary label with optional icons, supporting descriptions, a toggle, and status information. Its primary use is to present related entries in a consistent, scannable row; a row can indicate navigation, expose a setting, or communicate an item’s status according to the surrounding context.

Variants and Controls

-Status

• Default: the default row presentation.

• secondary: an alternate visual presentation. Its name does not define selected, hover, or disabled behavior; use according to the surrounding design’s hierarchy.

• errored: error-emphasis presentation with optional information icon and status chip.

• queued: queued-status presentation with optional information icon and status chip. Do not treat a queued item as disabled solely because of its visual styling.

Content and visibility controls:

• label: primary text; default is “Section Label”.

• has icon: shows the leading icon; default is true. Instance swaps the leading icon component.

• directional: shows the trailing navigation indicator; default is true.

• bottom description and right description: show supporting text below the label or on the right; both default to false. Replace their sample text when shown.

• has toggle: shows the switch; default is false.

• right icon: shows an additional trailing icon; default is false.

• has chip and info icon: show status elements in errored and queued variants; both default to true.

• These controls define visual content, not working navigation, switch behavior, or status transitions. Implement those behaviors separately.

Use Cases and Exceptions

Recommended usage:

• Navigation lists: use a clear destination label and retain the directional indicator when the row opens another view or details.
• Settings lists: show the toggle for a binary setting. Avoid combining a navigation indicator and toggle unless each action is clearly distinguished.
• Status lists: use queued for waiting items and errored for items requiring error attention. Make status understandable through text, not color alone.
• Supporting details: show a bottom description for explanatory text, or a right description for concise metadata. Keep the primary label easy to scan.
• Status chips: ensure the chip label matches the actual status. The errored variant currently includes a “Queued” sample chip; replace that sample with accurate error-status text before use.
• Use icons only when they clarify the entry or action. Avoid showing every optional control together when it creates competing actions or crowded content.
• In implementation, use link semantics for navigation and switch semantics for settings; provide accessible names for icon-only actions.

components.name: list-section
components.description:
What the Component Does?
Groups related list items into a single vertical section with an optional section title and bottom divider. Its primary use is to organize a menu or modal’s entries into clear, scannable groups while keeping row presentation consistent.

Variants and Controls
• Type=menu lists: the default section presentation. The sample content contains three list item instances with leading icons and trailing directional indicators, suitable for grouped navigation entries.

 type=modal lists: a section presentation for modal content. The sample rows use the secondary list item presentation with leading grip-style icons, right-side metadata, and trailing delete icons; directional indicators are hidden.
• list container slot: supplies the section’s list content. Both variants contain three sample rows; this is sample content, not a documented three-item limit.
• has title: shows or hides the header; default is true. Replace “Section title” with a descriptive group title. Title text is not exposed as a section-level text property.
• divider: shows or hides the bottom divider; default is true.

• Row labels, icons, metadata, toggles, and status presentations belong to the nested list items, not the section-level controls. Configure those through the list content.
• The section uses a vertical layout: header, list content, then divider.

• The variants define visual presentation only. Navigation, deletion, reordering, selection, and scrolling must be configured separately in implementation. A grip-style icon alone does not establish working drag-and-drop behavior.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use menu lists to group related destinations or actions within a menu or navigation surface. 

Keep directional indicators only when entries lead to another view or details.

• Use modal lists for grouped entries managed inside a modal, such as a collection with concise metadata and item-level removal actions.

• Give each section a short, descriptive title. Hide the title when the surrounding context already identifies the group clearly.

• Use the bottom divider to separate adjacent groups; hide it when another boundary already provides sufficient separation.

• Replace all sample labels and metadata with accurate content. Keep entries in the same section related and use a consistent row configuration for equivalent actions.

• Treat navigation and trailing actions as distinct interaction targets. In implementation, provide accessible names for icon-only actions and keyboard alternatives for any reordering interaction.

• Avoid using this section as a substitute for a data table when users need to compare multiple aligned fields. Define empty-state and long-list behavior in the surrounding design; neither is a section variant in this set.

components.name: Righthand Menu
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides application-defined subsection navigation for Business@Slalom. Its primary use is to show the sections belonging to the application selected in the left-hand platform menu. Switching the left-menu application must update this navigation to the corresponding application’s section list.

The documented applications are Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, and Taxonomy. Righthand Menu supplies the app-specific navigation composition; item styles and behaviors are defined by Righthand Navigation Item.

Variants and Controls
• Application: Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, Taxonomy. Select the value matching the active left-menu application.
• Collapsed=false: expanded, labeled navigation with a Collapse control.
• Collapsed=true: compact icon navigation with an Expand control.
• Each application supports both presentations, for six variants. Current Figma default: Application=Engagement Tracker, Collapsed=false.
• Collapsed is a variant axis, not an automatic responsive or working expansion control.
• Engagement Tracker sections, in supplied order: Engagement, Baseline, Collaborators, Workstreams, Tracker, EAC Summary, Changes, Financials, Insights, Pulse, Feedback.
• Slalom Chat sections, in supplied order: Chat, Chat History, Prompt Library, Digital Experts, Model Advisors, Graph Explorer, Settings.
• Taxonomy sections, in supplied order: Taxonomy, Locations, Enablement Roles, Changes.
• Each section is a nested Righthand Navigation Item. Configure its Label, State, and Collapsed presentation through that component; use its documentation as the source of item-state and interaction rules.
• Section icons come from Nav Icon through the nested navigation items. Keep each app section’s icon identity consistent across labeled and compact presentations.
• App switching, routing, selected-section updates, expansion, keyboard handling, and overflow must be configured in implementation. The variants do not automatically synchronize with the left menu.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Required usage:
• Use as the active application’s subsection navigation, not as the platform-level app selector. The left-hand menu selects the application; this menu selects a section within it.
• Match Application to the selected left-menu item and keep the right-navigation contents synchronized when the application changes. Do not display another app’s section list under the current app.
• Preserve the supplied app-specific section grouping and order unless product rules explicitly define an alternative. Do not merge all applications’ entries into one generic list.
• Set the active subsection through Righthand Navigation Item’s Selected state; use Default for other available entries and Hover for temporary feedback.
• Keep nested items’ Collapsed values consistent with the surrounding menu. Expansion changes presentation, not destinations or permissions.
• Use the named section icons from Nav Icon and the item component’s corresponding state treatment. Do not infer a new destination from reference artwork.
• Provide accessible section names in compact navigation, keyboard access, visible focus, and a current-destination indication. Label access must not depend only on pointer hover.
• Fit navigation to the available viewport and define overflow or responsive adaptation through product guidance. No breakpoint thresholds or mobile-specific variant are supplied.

Exceptions:
• Only Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, and Taxonomy have application variants in this set. Other Business@Slalom applications require a defined navigation composition; do not reuse an unrelated app’s list as a substitute.
• Righthand Navigation Item governs item styling and behavior. This container does not introduce independent item-state or action rules.

components.name: card_row-slot
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides a structured content row within the main card component. Its primary use is to group a title and description with relevant supporting information, using a text-and-chip, icon-led, or avatar-led presentation and an optional row-level action where supported.

Usage is restricted to the main card component. Despite its name, card_row-slot is a component set containing predefined row layouts, not an exposed content insertion slot or a standalone card.

Variants and Controls
The variant axis is named Property 1 and contains three values:
• card row_type01: an icon-led row with title/description content. The sample chip is hidden; an optional action is available below the row.
• card row_type02: the default text-led row with a visible supporting chip. This variant has no action button container.
• card row_type03: an avatar-led row with title/description content and an optional action below the row. The sample uses a graphic avatar; a separate initials container is hidden.
• has CTA: defaults to false and controls Button Container visibility in type01 and type03. It has no corresponding action container in type02.
• The optional action in type01 and type03 is an enabled, outlined sm button with Title Case text and no visible leading or trailing icons. Replace “Button Text” through the nested button’s Text property.
• Titles, descriptions, chip content, icons, and avatar artwork are configured through the relevant nested content. There are no equivalent top-level text, avatar-swap, chip-visibility, or content-slot properties.
• The visible sample chip in type02 reads “Default”; replace it with meaningful, accurate supporting information through the nested chip content.
• These variants define content composition, not selected, hover, or interaction states. Any row action, navigation, or status behavior must be configured separately in implementation.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use only inside the main card component’s content area to present a coherent item or related set of rows.
• Choose type01 when an icon clarifies the item, type02 when text and a chip are sufficient, or type03 when an avatar representation is relevant.
• Keep titles and descriptions consistent with the parent card’s subject. Replace sample text, icons, chips, and avatar artwork with appropriate content; do not infer an identity or status from sample graphics.
• Use the chip for concise metadata or status only when its meaning is clear. Do not rely on color alone to communicate status.
• Show the optional row action only when needed. Its sm sizing must follow the button family’s restriction to sections containing a list of actions that require buttons; otherwise use the parent card’s approved action composition.
• Keep row-level actions distinct from the main card’s CTA area. Do not assume enabling has CTA makes the row a fixed footer or a whole-card action group.
• Check content at the intended card width so titles, descriptions, icons, and actions remain readable and contained.
• In implementation, provide keyboard access and explicit action labels for interactive elements. Treat redundant icon or avatar artwork as decorative.

Exceptions:
• Scope restriction: card_row-slot is permitted only within the main card component. Do not use it independently, as a page-level list item, or in unrelated or specialized components.
• type02 does not support the optional CTA container; has CTA does not add an action to that variant.
• No exception to the main-card-only usage restriction is defined.

components.name: menu
components.description:
What the Component Does?

Displays a contextual list of specific actions from an activator in a designated area of the product.

Its primary use is to keep related actions accessible without showing the full action list at all times.

Menus can provide actions for a table, a container, a menu bar, or a floating button.

Variants and Controls

• type=iconleft: uses a FAB activator aligned to the left of the menu.

• type=icon Right: uses a FAB activator aligned to the right of the menu. These type names describe activator placement, not menu-row icon visibility.

• type=button: uses a labeled button activator.

• status=closed: hides the action list while retaining activator containers according to their visibility controls.

• status=opened: displays the action list.

• has button is a variant axis, not a Boolean visibility control. The available combinations are iconleft + true, icon Right + true, and button + false; each supports opened and closed. The button + false variants still contain a labeled button activator.

• The set contains six variants. Current Figma default: type=iconleft, has button=true, status=closed.

• top cta: shows the top activator container; default is true.

• bottom_cta: shows the bottom activator container; default is false. Choose the activator placement that matches the surrounding layout rather than showing both by default.

• left icon and right icon: control leading and trailing icons in the action rows; defaults are true and false respectively.

• Each sample menu contains six rows labeled “List item Label”. Replace sample labels and icons with context-specific actions; six rows is sample content, not a documented product limit. Row labels are not exposed as menu-level text properties, and this set has no content slot.

• These variants represent visual states. Opening, dismissal, action execution, keyboard navigation, tooltip behavior, and viewport-aware positioning must be configured separately in implementation.

Use Cases and Exceptions

Recommended usage:

• Tables: offer actions for the associated row or selected records. Make the action scope clear.

• Containers: group actions belonging to that container’s content, such as editing or managing the displayed item.

• Menu bars: provide related commands from a labeled activator.

• Floating buttons: reveal related actions from a prominent access point when a single direct action is insufficient. Follow the FAB’s usage guidance.

• Use concise, action-oriented labels and meaningful icons. Keep actions relevant to the activator’s context and distinguish destructive actions clearly.

• Keep the opened menu near its activator without clipping it or obscuring essential content.

• If an icon-only activator needs a tooltip, use it as supplemental explanation; give the activator its own accessible name. Coordinate tooltip and menu visibility in implementation so they do not compete.

• In implementation, expose the activator’s expanded state, support keyboard access to actions and Escape dismissal, and return focus to the activator when the menu closes.

• Do not hide the only discoverable route to a critical action in an ambiguous menu. Use a dialog or another dedicated surface for forms, long instructions, or multi-step tasks.

components.name: Tabs
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides an individual selectable tab for organizing related content at the same level of hierarchy. Use multiple instances together as a tab group to let users switch between associated content sections while maintaining page context.

Vuetify describes tabs as selectable items that reveal associated content and can also serve as page-level pseudo-navigation when tabs are links. This Figma component represents one tab item, not a complete tab group or its content panels.

Usage reference:
https://vuetifyjs.com/en/components/tabs/#usage

Variants and Controls
• State=Selected: identifies the active tab and its corresponding visible content.
• State=Unselected: represents an available tab that is not active.
• State=Disabled: represents an unavailable tab. Prevent activation in implementation; styling alone does not disable an action.
• Hover=Hover and Hover=No Hover: pointer-feedback presentations for Selected and Unselected. Disabled is supplied only with No Hover.
• The set contains five variants, not all six State/Hover combinations. Current Figma default is State=Disabled, Hover=No Hover; this is not a recommendation to make new tab groups disabled.
• Tab Label: exposed text property; default is “Tab Label”. Replace it with a concise description of the associated content.
• has icon: controls icon visibility; default is true.
• Icon: instance-swap property for the icon. Choose meaningful artwork rather than retaining the sample plus symbol without context.
• The supplied icon-and-label composition stacks the icon above the text. Hiding the icon provides a text-only presentation; no label-visibility control is exposed.
• Selection, content switching, destinations, keyboard behavior, group alignment, overflow, and responsive adaptation must be configured through the surrounding tab group and implementation.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use for peer content sections, not successive process steps or unrelated product destinations. Keep the selected tab and its visible panel synchronized, with one selected tab in a single-view group.
• Use clear, distinct labels and a consistent icon treatment across equivalent tabs. Keep hover feedback separate from persistent selection.
• Apply Disabled only when a tab is genuinely unavailable; do not use the component’s default state as the group’s initial availability rule.
• Vuetify supports start, center, and end alignment; fixed-width or growing tabs; vertical layouts; and centering the active tab. Select the group behavior according to product rules. These are implementation options, not extra variants in this set.
• Define overflow behavior instead of compressing labels until they become unreadable. Vuetify displays pagination controls for overflowing desktop tabs; mobile arrows require its show-arrows option. Its documented alternatives include an overflow menu and keeping the active tab visible.
• Vuetify supports icon-only tabs on mobile to conserve space. This Figma set does not expose label visibility, so do not assume that presentation is already available; use an approved composition with accessible names if required.
• When using tabs as page-level links, define the destinations and current-location behavior explicitly rather than treating every tab as a local panel switch.
• In implementation, use appropriate tab-list, tab, and panel semantics for local content switching; associate tabs with panels, expose selection, and support keyboard navigation with visible focus. Do not confuse hover with keyboard focus.

Exceptions:
• Disabled + Hover is not supplied. Do not imply an unavailable tab becomes actionable through hover.
• Complete tab groups, panels, overflow controls, icon-only mobile layouts, vertical groups, and responsive switching are not provided by this individual-item component.
• The separate Tab-slot component remains restricted to main card usage; that restriction does not make this reusable Tabs item main-card-only.
• Additional product-specific restrictions require explicit guidance.

components.name: selector-item
components.description:
What the Component Does
Displays one selectable option within a dropdown, autocomplete, or selection list. Use type=single for a label-only option and with description when supporting text is needed. Set Property 1 to default, hover, or selected to match the item’s interaction state. Use icon left and icon right to show optional leading or trailing icons.


Use Cases

• Label-only choices that are easy to distinguish.
• Choices that need a short description for clarification.
• Showing hover feedback and the currently selected option.


Exceptions

components.name: Lefthand Menu
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides the platform’s main navigation across its applications. This menu is restricted to the left side of the application layout and supplies a consistent access point for switching between platform modules.

The menu is the navigation container. Item-level behaviors and presentations are defined by the Lefthand Menu Nav Item component; use that component as the source of truth rather than defining separate behaviors in this container.

Variants and Controls
• Lefthand Menu is a single component, not a component set. It has no exposed top-level properties or variants.
• Its Icon Group arranges five nested Left-hand Menu Nav Item instances vertically. The sample order is Slalom Chat, Engagement Tracker, Taxonomy, connexus, and summit.
• Every sample item uses State=Unselected and Expansion=Collapsed. These are sample states, not a rule that all items remain unselected in the running application.
• Nested item State options: Unselected, Hover, Selected.
• Nested item Module options: Taxonomy, Engagement Tracker, summit, Slalom Chat, connexus.
• Nested item Expansion options: Collapsed, Expanded.
• These properties belong to Lefthand Menu Nav Item and are not exposed as container-level controls. Configure each nested item through the appropriate item properties.
• The sample container is a narrow icon rail. It does not expose a menu-wide expansion or responsive-breakpoint control.
• Navigation destinations, interaction triggers, selected-state updates, focus behavior, and expansion handling must follow the Lefthand Menu Nav Item contract and be configured in implementation. The container itself does not define working navigation.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Required usage:
• Place this menu only on the left as the main navigation across platform applications. Maintain a consistent location and module ordering according to platform rules.
• Use the matching Module value for each destination. Do not repurpose module icons for unrelated commands.
• Match the selected item to the current application. Use the item’s Selected state for the active module and its Hover presentation for pointer feedback; hover is not persistent selection.
• Apply Collapsed or Expanded presentations according to the item component’s defined behavior. Do not infer a new menu-wide expansion interaction from the available item variants.
• Keep this platform navigation separate from contextual action menus, account/avatar menus, and local card actions.
• In implementation, expose the menu as a navigation landmark, provide accessible destination names for icon-only items, indicate the current destination, and support keyboard navigation with visible focus.
• Follow product guidance for responsive placement and overflow. No mobile substitution, alternative position, or breakpoint threshold is defined by this component.

Exceptions:
• Placement restriction: this menu is only for the left side. Do not use it as right-side, top, or bottom navigation.
• Role restriction: this is the main platform-app navigation, not a general-purpose menu or local action list.
• Item behaviors must remain governed by Lefthand Menu Nav Item. No exception to the left-side/main-navigation scope is defined.

components.name: list-row-slot
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides a compact, structured information row within the main card component. Its primary use is to present a label and supporting text alongside an optional icon, chip, or score presentation so related card information can be scanned consistently.

Usage is restricted to the main card component. Despite its name, list-row-slot is a component set with predefined row content, not an exposed insertion slot or a general-purpose page list item.

Variants and Controls
• style=Type1: the default icon-led row, with title and subtitle stacked vertically and an optional trailing chip.
• style=Type2: a score-oriented row with a leading numeric sample, stacked title/subtitle, and trailing star graphics. The sample number is “4”; the set does not expose a score-value or rating-scale property.
• style=Type 3: an icon-led row with title and subtitle arranged horizontally. It has no trailing chip or score section.
• black icon: shows the alternate leading icon in Type1 and Type 3; default is false.
• blue icon: shows the blue leading icon in Type1 and Type 3; default is true. Choose one icon presentation at a time, or hide both when no icon is needed. These controls are not bound to Type2’s score graphics.
• has subtitle: controls supporting-text visibility in all three variants; default is true.
• has chip: controls the chip in Type1; default is true. Type2 and Type 3 contain no chip controlled by this property.
• Replace “List title”, “List Content”, “Subtitle”, and the chip’s “Default” text through the relevant nested content. There are no equivalent top-level text properties.
• Numeric values and star graphics in Type2 must be configured consistently through its content. Do not assume the sample establishes a universal score, scale, or working rating input.
• The set has no hover, selected, disabled, or action variants. Navigation, rating input, and other interactions are not established by the visual row structure.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use only in the main card component’s content area for related information rows.
• Use Type1 when a supporting chip adds useful metadata, Type2 when the product defines a meaningful score presentation, and Type 3 when inline supporting text fits the card’s layout.
• Keep labels concise and specific to the card’s subject. Hide subtitles or chips when they add no useful information.
• Use meaningful icons rather than retaining sample plus symbols without context. Do not infer an action from an icon alone.
• For Type2, define the metric and scale, ensure the number and stars agree, and provide an accessible text explanation. Do not communicate the score through color or star graphics alone.
• Check long labels and subtitles at the intended card width, especially Type 3’s horizontal text arrangement, to avoid collisions or clipping.
• Keep equivalent rows consistent within a card. Place card-level actions in the main card’s CTA area rather than repurposing this information row as a button group.
• Treat rows as informational unless a product-approved interaction is explicitly defined; provide keyboard access and clear semantics for any interactive use.

Exceptions:
• Scope restriction: list-row-slot is permitted only within the main card component. Do not use it independently, in page navigation, or within unrelated or specialized components.
• Chip visibility applies only to Type1; icon-color controls apply only to Type1 and Type 3. Type2’s score content requires separate configuration.
• No exception to the main-card-only usage restriction is defined.

components.name: bottom nav
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides Slalom Chat subsection navigation at tablet and mobile breakpoints. It replaces the app’s desktop Righthand Menu while preserving the same section access points, destinations, permissions, and navigation behavior.

When the layout changes from desktop to tablet, hide the right navigation and show bottom nav. Restore the right navigation when returning to desktop. Preserve the current section across the switch; changing layout must not navigate the user to a different section.

Variants and Controls
• size: xl, lg, md, sm. These are navigation-layout presentations, not button sizes or fixed implementation widths.
• xl and lg: wider presentations for displaying the full navigation list when labels fit on one line.
• md: compact presentation with three navigation items and More, with labels.
• sm: compact icon-only presentation with three navigation items and More.
• has CTA=False: the version currently in use, without the centered CTA. Use this for current Slalom Chat implementations.
• has CTA=true: the centered-CTA version, documented for future implementations only. Do not activate it as part of the current navigation pattern.
• has CTA is a variant axis with exact values False and true, not a Boolean property.
• status=default: standard presentation, available at all four sizes with or without CTA.
• status=digital experts: a future CTA-related presentation showing a contextual action list. Available only with has CTA=true at all four sizes; it does not define a status variant for every Chat section.
• The set contains 12 variants. Current Figma default: size=sm, status=default, has CTA=False.
• Nested bottom bar item instances supply destination labels, icons, label visibility, and selected/default states. Follow that component’s documentation for item styling and controls.
• Sample widths are xl=960 px, lg=744 px, md=500 px, and sm=375 px. These are sample dimensions, not a complete definition of tablet/desktop breakpoint thresholds.
• Sample labels and icon artwork are placeholders. Populate the complete approved Chat destination set; sample item counts must not remove access points that exist in the right navigation.
• Responsive switching, routing, selection updates, More disclosure, and bottom-sheet behavior must be configured in implementation. Visual variants alone do not establish these behaviors.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Required responsive usage:
• Larger tablet layouts: show all navigation items distributed to fill the bar width, with labels on one line. Do not leave arbitrary gaps or wrap labels to accommodate the full list.
• Width 500 px or less: use the compact structure with the first three navigation items in the approved product order, followed by More. Move the remaining destinations into the More bottom sheet.
• If a wider tablet layout cannot fit all items with single-line labels, use the same three-items-plus-More overflow structure instead of clipping, wrapping, or dropping destinations.
• Width 375 px through 500 px, inclusive: retain labels with the compact structure. Width below 375 px: hide item labels and show icons only, retaining the same three navigation items plus More. The label-hiding rule begins below 375 px, not at 375 px.
• More opens a bottom sheet containing every destination omitted from the bar. Preserve the same labels, destination meanings, permissions, and navigation outcomes as the Chat right navigation; More is an overflow trigger, not a new content section.
• Keep the complete destination set reachable through either the visible bar or the bottom sheet. Preserve the active destination when it moves into overflow, and provide a clear indication of the current section without treating More as a destination itself.
• Configure navigation using the same application rules as Righthand Menu and Righthand Navigation Item, while using bottom bar item for the bottom presentation.
• Provide accessible destination names when labels are hidden, keyboard access and visible focus, current-destination semantics, and an accessible More trigger. Apply bottom-sheet dismissal and focus handling to the overflow experience.

Exceptions:
• Current scope is Slalom Chat at tablet and mobile breakpoints only. Do not use this bar for other apps or as the desktop navigation without explicit product approval.
• The centered-CTA versions and digital experts CTA-related status are future documentation, not currently enabled patterns.
• The sm sample is 375 px wide and already hides labels; the required usage rule hides labels only below 375 px. Apply the documented threshold when implementing rather than copying that sample state at exactly 375 px.
• Overflow changes presentation only: it must never remove navigation access or introduce different permissions. No exception to the three-items-plus-More structure at compact widths is defined.

components.name: modal
components.description:
What the Component Does?

Presents focused information, a decision, or a task in a dialog without requiring users to leave the current product context. 
Use dialogs to ensure users understand relevant product information, respond to important warnings or urgent decisions, or enter data and perform system-related tasks.


Variants and Controls

• type=alert: informs users about important warnings or decisions requiring urgent attention. Keep the message and response focused on the immediate issue.

• type=data: supports information and knowledge introduction, including data definitions, terminology, tutorials, and guidance; also supports relevant data entry and task workflows that need more content space.

• type=announcement: highlights relevant launches or information users need to know, such as policies or new features. Uses a distinct banner-style header.

• rounded corner: a variant axis with values true and false. The set contains both treatments, but permitted usage is restricted to rounded corner=true for alert, data, and announcement. 

Use a 24 px corner radius (radius-xl) and 24 px dialog content padding on all sides (pa-6). 

The 24 px radius is corner rounding, not border stroke thickness. Do not use rounded corner=false or override these radius and padding values.


• Current Figma default: type=alert, rounded corner=true.

• content slot: supplies the dialog body. Insert the relevant information, warning, form, or task content; sample bodies are empty.

• CTA Section: supplies response or task actions; empty in the samples.

• Show CTA Section: shows or hides the action section in all three types; default is true.

• close: shows or hides the trailing close icon in alert and data variants; default is true. 

Announcement variants have no close icon bound to this control, so it does not provide announcement dismissal.

• has icon: shows or hides the leading header icon in alert and data variants; default is true. It is not bound to an icon in announcement variants.

• upper case and Sentence Case: control alternative title text visibility in data variants; defaults are false and true respectively. Show one title presentation at a time and supply the correct title wording. 

These controls are not general text-case controls for every dialog type.

• Titles are not exposed as component-level text properties. Replace sample header titles through the appropriate text content.

• The dialog organizes header, body, and action content vertically. Sample dimensions are not documented responsive breakpoint rules.

• Backdrop, opening, dismissal, focus handling, validation, submission, and scrolling must be configured separately in implementation; this set contains no open/closed or persistent-dialog variants.

Use Cases and Exceptions

• Use only the rounded-corner version: rounded corner=true, 24 px corner radius (radius-xl), and 24 px padding (pa-6). Apply this rule to every dialog type, regardless of its informational, warning, announcement, or task purpose.

Recommended usage:
• Product information: use data for definitions, terminology, tutorials, or guidance; use announcement when a policy, legal update, launch, or new feature needs prominent awareness. Choose based on the purpose, not merely the amount of text.

• Urgent warnings or decisions: use alert. State the issue, consequence, and required decision clearly; give response actions explicit labels.

• Data entry and system tasks: use data. Include clear field labels, relevant instructions, validation feedback, and actions appropriate to completing or cancelling the task.

• Populate content slot and CTA Section with a coherent task or message. Hide an unused CTA section only when another clear dismissal or completion route exists.

• Follow the button family’s hierarchy and size rules. Contained actions are for standalone highest emphasis; for three-action modals or alerts, a negative outlined md button may serve as the second-hierarchy action.

• Provide a clear, product-approved dismissal route. Hiding a close icon does not make a dialog persistent, and critical decisions must not be accidentally bypassed by an unspecified dismissal behavior.

• In implementation, give the dialog an accessible title, move focus into it, contain keyboard focus while modal, and restore focus to the trigger on dismissal. Define Escape and outside-click behavior according to the task and unsaved-data requirements.

• Keep content readable within the available viewport and define scrolling for long content. Use a dedicated page for lengthy or complex workflows that do not need a dialog.

• Avoid interrupting users with a dialog for routine information that can remain inline, and avoid stacking dialogs for unrelated tasks.

Exceptions:

• Announcement does not expose the same close-icon and leading-icon behavior as alert and data; provide any required dismissal through an explicit action or approved surrounding behavior.

• No exception to the required rounded version, 24 px radius (radius-xl), or 24 px padding (pa-6) is defined. Any exception requires explicit product approval.

components.name: list-section
components.description:
What the Component Does?
Groups related list items into a single vertical section with an optional section title and bottom divider. Its primary use is to organize a menu or modal’s entries into clear, scannable groups while keeping row presentation consistent.

Variants and Controls
• Type=menu lists: the default section presentation. The sample content contains three list item instances with leading icons and trailing directional indicators, suitable for grouped navigation entries.

 type=modal lists: a section presentation for modal content. The sample rows use the secondary list item presentation with leading grip-style icons, right-side metadata, and trailing delete icons; directional indicators are hidden.
• list container slot: supplies the section’s list content. Both variants contain three sample rows; this is sample content, not a documented three-item limit.
• has title: shows or hides the header; default is true. Replace “Section title” with a descriptive group title. Title text is not exposed as a section-level text property.
• divider: shows or hides the bottom divider; default is true.

• Row labels, icons, metadata, toggles, and status presentations belong to the nested list items, not the section-level controls. Configure those through the list content.
• The section uses a vertical layout: header, list content, then divider.

• The variants define visual presentation only. Navigation, deletion, reordering, selection, and scrolling must be configured separately in implementation. A grip-style icon alone does not establish working drag-and-drop behavior.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use menu lists to group related destinations or actions within a menu or navigation surface. 

Keep directional indicators only when entries lead to another view or details.

• Use modal lists for grouped entries managed inside a modal, such as a collection with concise metadata and item-level removal actions.

• Give each section a short, descriptive title. Hide the title when the surrounding context already identifies the group clearly.

• Use the bottom divider to separate adjacent groups; hide it when another boundary already provides sufficient separation.

• Replace all sample labels and metadata with accurate content. Keep entries in the same section related and use a consistent row configuration for equivalent actions.

• Treat navigation and trailing actions as distinct interaction targets. In implementation, provide accessible names for icon-only actions and keyboard alternatives for any reordering interaction.

• Avoid using this section as a substitute for a data table when users need to compare multiple aligned fields. Define empty-state and long-list behavior in the surrounding design; neither is a section variant in this set.

components.name: button
components.description:
What the Component Does?
Provides a reusable button for initiating a user action, with labeled and icon-only presentations. Variants control visual emphasis, size, and interaction-state appearance.

Properties:
• size: lg, md, sm.
• variant: contained_button, outlined, text, Plain, neutral_outlined, icon, icon contained.
• status: enabled, disabled, hover, pressed. The sync status displays a loading indicator and is available only for contained_button and neutral_outlined, in all three sizes.

• Text sets the label (default: “Button”). icon-left and icon right control optional leading and trailing icons on labeled variants; both default to true. All button labels are Title Case by default (title case=true; uppercase=false).
• Default usage: size=md, variant=contained_button, status=enabled.
• These variants represent visual states; application behavior must be implemented separately.

Use Cases

Recommended usage:
• contained_button: a prominent primary action, such as Save or Submit.
• outlined: a secondary action that needs a visible boundary without a filled background.
• neutral_outlined: a secondary or supporting action with neutral visual emphasis, such as Cancel.
• text: a low-emphasis action alongside more prominent buttons.
• Plain: a minimal, neutral action within supporting content.
• icon: a compact icon-only action in a toolbar or repeated row.
• icon contained: an icon-only action that needs stronger filled emphasis.
• md: the default button size. Use for actions unless one of the restricted size use cases below applies.
• lg: use only when the button is beside a field.
• sm: use only in sections or modals containing a list of actions that require buttons.
• Keep equivalent actions consistently sized.
• Use enabled for an available action, disabled for an unavailable action, hover for pointer-over feedback, and pressed for active press feedback. Use sync to represent an action in progress where that combination exists.
• Write a concise, action-oriented label in Title Case by default. Include icons only when they clarify the action. Give icon-only buttons an accessible name in implementation; do not rely on the icon alone.
• Use a link for ordinary destination navigation and a selection control for persistent choices rather than substituting a button.

Exceptions

components.name: drawer
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides a focused surface for contextual information, data entry, or a system task while retaining the surrounding page context. 


The drawer separates a header, central content area, and bottom action area so users can access the full content without losing the main actions.

Required responsive behavior:

• Desktop: use size=desktop only at desktop breakpoints. Drawer width must be 90% of the current viewport width at the active desktop breakpoint and adapt as the viewport changes; do not hard-code the sample width.

• Tablet: use size=tablet at tablet breakpoints, following the product’s tablet layout rules. Tablet is a separate presentation, not a mobile layout; mobile’s full-width and bottom-overlay restrictions do not apply.

• Mobile: use size=mobile at mobile breakpoints. Drawer width must be 100% of the viewport, with a bottom-anchored presentation that overlays the page to the bottom edge.

• For long content, allow only the central internal content area to scroll vertically. Keep the drawer within the available viewport rather than growing the entire surface beyond it.

Variants and Controls

• size: desktop, tablet, mobile. The default variant is desktop. These variants define layout presentations, not open/closed states.

• size=tablet: use at tablet breakpoints with tablet-specific sizing and placement according to product rules. 


Do not apply mobile’s 100% width or bottom-anchored overlay rule to tablet. 


Tablet may also be used on desktop only under the documented limited-content exception. 


Tablet width percentages and breakpoint thresholds are not specified here.

• header: supplies the drawer heading and any relevant header content.

• content: supplies the central body. Use this as the vertically scrollable region when content exceeds the available height.

• button set: supplies the bottom action area. Keep this area fixed at the bottom of the drawer and outside the scrolling content so the main CTAs remain visible.

• has CTA Section: controls button set visibility and defaults to true. Required usage keeps it true; do not hide the action area for the drawer experience described here.

• All three slots are empty in the samples. Populate them with the intended heading, content, and actions.

• Sample dimensions are not fixed usage dimensions. Responsive widths, bottom anchoring, scrolling, fixed footer behavior, dismissal, and task actions must be configured in implementation; the presence of slots alone does not establish these behaviors.

Use Cases and Exceptions

• Use for a contextual task or information flow that benefits from an overlay while maintaining page context.

• Populate the header with a clear title and the central content with one coherent task or topic.

• Keep the button set at the bottom and fixed throughout the experience, including when central content is long or scrolled.

• Place the main action on the right using a contained button (contained_button), size=md.

• Place Exit or Cancel on the left using a neutral outlined button (neutral_outlined), size=md. All buttons in the drawer action area must be md.

• When content grows, expand its internal scrollable content extent, not the full drawer height. Reserve visible space for the footer so it never covers the final content or scrolls out of reach.

• Preserve 90% responsive width for size=desktop and 100% for size=mobile. Use size=tablet on desktop only under the documented exception. Use the product’s breakpoint definitions; no numeric breakpoint thresholds are supplied by this component guidance.

• In implementation, provide clear action labels, keyboard access, visible focus, and a dismissal policy appropriate to unsaved data. For a modal overlay, manage focus within the drawer and restore it to the trigger on dismissal.

Exceptions:

• Desktop exception: size=tablet may be used at desktop breakpoints only when the drawer content is not large and the information behind the drawer needs to remain visible. 

Use size=desktop with its 90% responsive width for other desktop cases. This exception does not change the fixed bottom action area, md button sizing, or central-only vertical scrolling.

components.name: semantic Buttons
components.description:
What the Component Does

Provides action buttons with negative or positive semantic emphasis. Use negative for destructive actions such as Remove or Delete; use positive when an action needs positive semantic emphasis.

As with the main buttons, contained_button provides the highest visual hierarchy and is used only when the action is standalone. Outlined provides lower emphasis for actions within tables, lists, and action groups.

Available variants and controls:
• semantic: negative, positive.
• variant: contained_button, outlined.
• Size: lg, md, sm.
• status: default (available action), hover (pointer-over feedback), pressed (active press feedback), disable (unavailable action).
• All 48 combinations of semantic, variant, Size, and status are available.
• label controls the button text (default: “Button”). icon left and icon right control optional icons; both default to true.
• Labels are Title Case by default (Title Case=true; Upper Case=false), consistent with the main buttons.
• Status variants represent visual states; application behavior must be implemented separately.

Use Cases and Exceptions

Hierarchy and size guidance:
• Standalone actions: use contained_button only when the action stands alone and requires the highest emphasis.
• lg: use only when the button is beside a field, consistent with the main buttons.

Negative actions:
• Highlighted Remove or Delete action in a section: use negative + contained_button + md when the action is standalone and needs prominence.
• Tables or lists: negative + outlined + md is the suggested combination for Remove or Delete actions.
• Button lists: negative + outlined + sm is the suggested combination. Keep sm usage within sections or modals containing a list of actions that require buttons, consistent with the main buttons.
• Modals or alerts with three actions: negative + outlined + md can serve as the second-hierarchy button. Do not use a contained negative button within this action group.
• Use a clear, action-oriented label that identifies what will be removed or deleted. Include icons only when they clarify the action.

What the Component Does
Provides application-defined subsection navigation for Business@Slalom. Its primary use is to show the sections belonging to the application selected in the left-hand platform menu. Switching the left-menu application must update this navigation to the corresponding application’s section list.

The documented applications are Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, and Taxonomy. Righthand Menu supplies the app-specific navigation composition; item styles and behaviors are defined by Righthand Navigation Item.

Variants and Controls
• Application: Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, Taxonomy. Select the value matching the active left-menu application.
• Collapsed=false: expanded, labeled navigation with a Collapse control.
• Collapsed=true: compact icon navigation with an Expand control.
• Each application supports both presentations, for six variants. Current Figma default: Application=Engagement Tracker, Collapsed=false.
• Collapsed is a variant axis, not an automatic responsive or working expansion control.
• Engagement Tracker sections, in supplied order: Engagement, Baseline, Collaborators, Workstreams, Tracker, EAC Summary, Changes, Financials, Insights, Pulse, Feedback.
• Slalom Chat sections, in supplied order: Chat, Chat History, Prompt Library, Digital Experts, Model Advisors, Graph Explorer, Settings.
• Taxonomy sections, in supplied order: Taxonomy, Locations, Enablement Roles, Changes.
• Each section is a nested Righthand Navigation Item. Configure its Label, State, and Collapsed presentation through that component; use its documentation as the source of item-state and interaction rules.
• Section icons come from Nav Icon through the nested navigation items. Keep each app section’s icon identity consistent across labeled and compact presentations.
• App switching, routing, selected-section updates, expansion, keyboard handling, and overflow must be configured in implementation. The variants do not automatically synchronize with the left menu.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Required usage:
• Use as the active application’s subsection navigation, not as the platform-level app selector. The left-hand menu selects the application; this menu selects a section within it.
• Match Application to the selected left-menu item and keep the right-navigation contents synchronized when the application changes. Do not display another app’s section list under the current app.
• Preserve the supplied app-specific section grouping and order unless product rules explicitly define an alternative. Do not merge all applications’ entries into one generic list.
• Set the active subsection through Righthand Navigation Item’s Selected state; use Default for other available entries and Hover for temporary feedback.
• Keep nested items’ Collapsed values consistent with the surrounding menu. Expansion changes presentation, not destinations or permissions.
• Use the named section icons from Nav Icon and the item component’s corresponding state treatment. Do not infer a new destination from reference artwork.
• Provide accessible section names in compact navigation, keyboard access, visible focus, and a current-destination indication. Label access must not depend only on pointer hover.
• Fit navigation to the available viewport and define overflow or responsive adaptation through product guidance. No breakpoint thresholds or mobile-specific variant are supplied.

Exceptions:
• Only Engagement Tracker, Slalom Chat, and Taxonomy have application variants in this set. Other Business@Slalom applications require a defined navigation composition; do not reuse an unrelated app’s list as a substitute.
• Righthand Navigation Item governs item styling and behavior. This container does not introduce independent item-state or action rules.

components.name: card/model advisor
components.description:
What the Component Does
Presents a model’s identity, description, usage information, supported file information, and available tools to help users compare and choose models within Slalom Chat’s Model Advisor sections.

This is a specialized card, not a general-purpose content card. Its permitted scope is Model Advisor sections in Slalom Chat only.

Variants and Controls
The set contains four specific combinations:
• status=default, full description=false, supported files=true: the compact resting presentation. The CTA section is hidden by default.
• status=hover-selected, full description=false, supported files=true: the combined hover/selected presentation with a visible “Select Model” action. The name combines two concepts; it does not provide separate hover and selected variants.
• status=expanded file section, full description=false, supported files=true: displays expanded supported-file details with a “Select Model” action.
• status=expanded description, full description=true, supported files=false: displays the longer description and “Close Description” affordance with a “Select Model” action.
• full description and supported files are variant axes with string values true/false, not independent Boolean switches. Use the available combinations; do not assume every combination exists.
• Current Figma default: status=default, full description=false, supported files=true.
• model name and model description: exposed text controls. Replace the sample model name and description with accurate, approved model content.
• support images, support audio, support video, and support app: exposed Boolean capability controls; all default to true. Verify that the displayed indicators and accompanying text match the actual model’s supported capabilities.
• has CTA: defaults to false and controls the CTA section in the default variant. The other three variants have visible CTA sections without that visibility binding; do not assume this control hides their actions.
• Budget, file-size limits, file extensions, accepted languages, and tool indicators are supplied within the card content rather than exposed as equivalent top-level text properties. Update them consistently for the represented model.
• Description expansion, file-section expansion, model selection, and persistence of selected state must be configured in implementation. Visual variants alone do not establish these behaviors.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use only in Slalom Chat Model Advisor sections to help users evaluate a model’s suitability and select an available model.
• Keep equivalent information in a consistent order across model cards so descriptions, usage limits, file support, and tools can be compared.
• Use the compact presentation for scanning, expanded description for deeper explanation, and expanded file section for compatibility details.
• Use “Select Model” for the explicit selection action. Define hover feedback and persistent selection separately in implementation rather than assuming the combined hover-selected variant establishes both.
• Treat every model capability and limit as evidence-bearing content. Do not copy the sample model description, budget, 4.5 MB file-size value, extensions, or languages as universal model facts.
• Keep capability indicators, text lists, and expanded details consistent. Verify sample file-extension spellings against approved model support data before use.
• Provide keyboard access and accessible labels for selection, expansion controls, and capability icons. Make selected state understandable without relying on styling alone.

Exceptions:
• Product and section restriction: this card is only for Model Advisor sections in Slalom Chat. Do not reuse it in other products, other Slalom Chat sections, or generic card layouts.
• This specialized card uses its own four presentation combinations and model-specific information structure; do not assume the general card’s variants or content slots apply.
• No broader usage exception is defined.

components.name: list-section
components.description:
What the Component Does?
Groups related list items into a single vertical section with an optional section title and bottom divider. Its primary use is to organize a menu or modal’s entries into clear, scannable groups while keeping row presentation consistent.

Variants and Controls
• Type=menu lists: the default section presentation. The sample content contains three list item instances with leading icons and trailing directional indicators, suitable for grouped navigation entries.

 type=modal lists: a section presentation for modal content. The sample rows use the secondary list item presentation with leading grip-style icons, right-side metadata, and trailing delete icons; directional indicators are hidden.
• list container slot: supplies the section’s list content. Both variants contain three sample rows; this is sample content, not a documented three-item limit.
• has title: shows or hides the header; default is true. Replace “Section title” with a descriptive group title. Title text is not exposed as a section-level text property.
• divider: shows or hides the bottom divider; default is true.

• Row labels, icons, metadata, toggles, and status presentations belong to the nested list items, not the section-level controls. Configure those through the list content.
• The section uses a vertical layout: header, list content, then divider.

• The variants define visual presentation only. Navigation, deletion, reordering, selection, and scrolling must be configured separately in implementation. A grip-style icon alone does not establish working drag-and-drop behavior.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Recommended usage:
• Use menu lists to group related destinations or actions within a menu or navigation surface. 

Keep directional indicators only when entries lead to another view or details.

• Use modal lists for grouped entries managed inside a modal, such as a collection with concise metadata and item-level removal actions.

• Give each section a short, descriptive title. Hide the title when the surrounding context already identifies the group clearly.

• Use the bottom divider to separate adjacent groups; hide it when another boundary already provides sufficient separation.

• Replace all sample labels and metadata with accurate content. Keep entries in the same section related and use a consistent row configuration for equivalent actions.

• Treat navigation and trailing actions as distinct interaction targets. In implementation, provide accessible names for icon-only actions and keyboard alternatives for any reordering interaction.

• Avoid using this section as a substitute for a data table when users need to compare multiple aligned fields. Define empty-state and long-list behavior in the surrounding design; neither is a section variant in this set.

components.name: avatar menu
components.description:
What the Component Does?

Provides the specialized avatar-triggered menu in the product’s top navigation. 

This is a specific use case of the menu pattern: it gives users a consistent access point for their identity information, product help, user preferences, and policy access, rather than actions belonging to a table row or local container.

The avatar remains visible as the activator. The opened panel organizes user information at the top, action content in the middle, and supporting information at the bottom.

Variants and Controls

• status=Default: the default, closed presentation; the avatar is visible and the menu panel is hidden.

• status=opened: displays the avatar and menu panel.

• top slot: supplies the panel’s top content. The sample contains “name.lastname@slalom.com”; replace it with the relevant user identity information.

• Content Slot: supplies the menu’s main action content. It is empty in the sample; populate it with the account or user-level actions required by the product.

• bottom section: supplies supporting footer content. The sample contains the Slalom security badge and “Always review results for accuracy.” Keep security and disclaimer wording aligned with approved product guidance.
• has top slot: shows or hides the top slot in the opened variant; default is true.

• divider: shows or hides the controlled Divider frame in the opened variant; default is true. A separate divider line remains visible, so this property does not remove every separator.

• bottom slot: shows or hides the bottom section in the opened variant; default is true. This is a Boolean control, distinct from the bottom section content slot.

• The avatar contains sample initials “ED”. Initials and user identity text are not exposed as component-level text properties; configure them through the relevant content.

• These two variants represent visual states. Activation, action execution, dismissal, keyboard navigation, focus management, and viewport-aware positioning must be configured separately in implementation.

Use Cases and Exceptions

• Place this specialized menu in the top navigation as the avatar-based access point for the current user’s account and related actions.

• Use the top area to identify the current user and the central Content Slot for product-approved account actions, such as profile or account settings when those actions exist in the product.

• Keep actions relevant to product help, the user, preferences, or policy access. Use the general menu component for contextual actions in tables, containers, menu bars, or floating-button action lists.

• Replace sample initials and identity text with accurate user content. Do not expose unnecessary personal information in the menu.

• Use concise action labels and group related entries consistently. Preserve approved security and accuracy messaging where required; do not infer security guarantees from the sample badge.

• Keep the opened panel visually associated with its avatar and within the available viewport, without obscuring essential navigation.

• In implementation, give the avatar activator an accessible name, expose its expanded state, support keyboard access and Escape dismissal, and return focus to the avatar when the menu closes.

• Use a dedicated page or dialog for lengthy settings forms or multi-step account tasks rather than placing them inside this menu.

Special applications — reviewed examples:

• Shared structure: show user identity at the top; product-specific help when applicable; “Browse Help for all Products”; “User Preferences”; “Acceptable Use Policy”; then the security badge and accuracy disclaimer. Separate related groups with dividers and omit empty groups.

• Slalom Chat: label the product-help group “Slalom Chat” and include “Tutorials” and “Contact our Team”. Include “Dark Mode” and “Settings” under “User Preferences”. Keep cross-product help and policy access separate from the product-specific group.

• Engagement Tracker: label the product-help group “Engagement Tracker” and include “Tutorials”, “Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)”, and “Contact our Team”. The reviewed examples include “Dark Mode” under “User Preferences” but no “Settings” row; do not add Settings solely to match Slalom Chat.

• Shared/minimal application: when no product-specific help group is needed, omit that group. Retain “Browse Help for all Products”, “User Preferences” with “Dark Mode”, and “Acceptable Use Policy”, followed by the security badge and accuracy disclaimer. Do not reserve blank space for omitted product rows.

• Composition: supply the identity through top slot, application-specific list sections through Content Slot, and approved supporting messaging through bottom section. These are content compositions of the existing avatar menu, not additional status variants.

• Avatar treatment: the reviewed Slalom Chat and minimal examples use initials; Engagement Tracker uses a profile photo. Use the correct available user identity representation and retain the same top-navigation activator role.

• Light and dark presentations: preserve the application’s content and grouping when changing theme. Adapt the menu surface, text, icons, dividers, and avatar treatment to the surrounding theme while retaining readability.

• Dark Mode control: bind the switch to the actual application theme in implementation. The Slalom Chat and Engagement Tracker examples show Off in light mode and On in dark mode. The minimal dark example currently shows Off despite its dark appearance; do not copy that sample as a theme-state rule. Resolve the mismatch when implementing the control.

• Interaction scope: treat Dark Mode as a setting control, and help, Settings, and policy rows as their respective destinations or actions. A trailing chevron does not establish behavior; configure each supported action explicitly.

• Footer: preserve the reviewed “Slalom InfoSec Safe and Secure” badge and “Always review results for accuracy.” wording only where approved and applicable to the product. Do not derive new security claims from the sample.

components.name: footer
components.description:
What the Component Does
Provides Connexus users with access to the InfoSec Safe and Secure information modal and the Acceptable Use Policy, alongside the reminder “Always review results for accuracy.” Its primary use is to keep these security-information and policy access points available in the application footer.

The footer experience has migrated to the top-navigation avatar menu in the other platform applications. This footer remains only in Connexus, where it continues to provide the security-information and policy access points. It is not a general platform footer; use the avatar menu for the migrated experience in other applications.

Variants and Controls
• type=desktop: the default horizontal presentation, with the Slalom security badge and footer text arranged across the footer. A separator divides the accuracy reminder from the policy text.
• type=mobile: a vertically stacked presentation, with the security badge above the accuracy reminder and policy-link area.
• type is the only exposed property. There are no top-level text, link-visibility, content-slot, hover, or modal-open controls.
• Both variants contain the nested slalom security badge using its slalom info sec presentation and the label “Slalom InfoSec Safe and Secure”.
• Both contain “Always review results for accuracy.” and “Acceptable Use Policy.”. Preserve approved wording rather than treating security and legal copy as generic placeholder text.
• The mobile sample also contains “Contact Us”. That additional link is outside the scope supplied for this footer; its presence does not define an approved destination or interaction.
• Modal opening, policy access, keyboard focus, responsive switching, and footer positioning must be configured in implementation. The visual badge and text alone do not provide working access.

Use Cases and Exceptions
Required usage:
• Use only in Connexus as the footer access point for security information and the Acceptable Use Policy.
• Activating the security-information badge must open the approved InfoSec Safe and Secure modal. Do not infer new security guarantees from the badge wording.
• Activating Acceptable Use Policy must provide access to the approved policy content. This component does not define whether that content opens in a modal or another destination; follow Connexus product guidance.
• Keep the accuracy reminder informational unless an explicit product-approved action is defined.
• Choose desktop or mobile according to Connexus layout rules. Keep both required access points available when changing presentation; do not drop policy access to fit a smaller width.
• Ensure footer content remains readable without collisions or clipping and is not obscured by navigation or overlays. No fixed/sticky positioning or tablet-specific variant is defined by this set.
• In implementation, provide accessible names, appropriate link/button semantics, keyboard access, and visible focus. Apply dialog focus management and dismissal behavior to the security modal.

Exceptions:
• Product restriction: this footer remains only in Connexus. Other applications use the migrated avatar navigation menu experience; do not reintroduce this footer or duplicate those access points in a separate footer there.
• The mobile sample’s additional Contact Us text is not part of the defined security/policy scope. Do not infer required functionality from it; any additional footer action needs approval.
• No exception permits removing the required security-information or policy access points from the approved Connexus footer experience.
